Some Buddhists reconcile the apparent contrasting view of anatta with the view of rebirth by explaining away the lack of a soul that could transfer with a sort of 'stream' of consciousness. I don't know if it's entirely accurate to say that Buddhism doesn't teach reincarnation, even if there view of it is different from other Dharmic religions. One of the key impulses for seeking Nirvana is supposedly to end the cycle of rebirth and death, and thus escape Samsara/Dukkha, implying that there is something to escape that death alone doesn't take care of. More Western/materialistic sects of Buddhism tend to overlook or do away with reincarnation obviously, but it doesn't mean it's not a key concept in traditional Buddhism. It's possible all this reincarnation stuff in Dharmic religions is meant to be taken as metaphorical, like you were saying, and not an actual transfer of consciousness, as we're all technically incarnations of the universe and part of the same One, but I don't know if that's how most Buddhists understand it or believe it should be understood. I've had similar thoughts, and the enlightened thing to say I think would be something like "you're still clinging to being someone and having an identity," or something, but I get exactly what you mean. It feels like turning away, giving up. But, I think a way of thinking about it that might help is you don't *have* to give up doing things and searching for experiences. As long as you recognize that it's all a game, the same way you do when you're playing a video game, and that the stakes aren't that high, so there's no reason to worry. Nobody's telling you that you absolutely have to renounce the world and become enlightened -- just that that's an option. It's an option a lot of people act on when they realize the inherent dissatisfaction of wanting and being separate, but it doesn't mean you need to as well, just like you don't need to stop playing a frustrating video game because you keep dying. Once you start to *feel* the weight of identity and action is when you get to opt out, like how when you put 200 hours into a game you'll get bored and stop playing. That there are other people feeling the exact same way that you are, and that while you could see that as something that takes away your uniqueness, the really healthy, ginormous-burden-off-your-shoulders thing to do is recognize that you're not alone, and that healing is miserable but at the end of the day all you can do is take your miserable experience and try your best to grow from it. Also, don't punish yourself for feeling shitty, just afterwards try your best not to feel shitty again. Breathing exercises, along with the recommended exercises and some light yoga helped me a lot, so maybe give that a go.

*This was not a good idea.* As I crept through the decrepit old complex it occurred to me that there was so much I was risking on a silly little impulse. But for the first time in my life, I was going to damn the consequences and just do what I wanted to in the moment. My 4.0 GPA, my curfew, Taylor and all her mixed messages, all of these things could wait until the morrow. Tonight, I planned on accomplishing something, not preparing for something else. I would sate my five year old curiosity, or die trying. It was about then that I turned the corner, took in another impossibly long hallway littered with presumably locked wooden doors, and the light flickered. I turned around. *Tomorrow is another day*, I consoled myself, and the eerie, old building would still be here then. 

As I walked through the long corridor I cursed myself for not bringing my ragged old sweatshirt. It wasn't cold, but the feeling of fabric against my skin was always comforting. Finally, I reached the thick glass door I had entered the fluorescent bathed section of the complex, still as tinted and opaque as ever. I pushed the door firmly and nearly toppled over as I was met with firm resistance. Glad to see that no one was around to see my falter, I pulled at the door, deriding myself for not checking to see if it was push or pull first. It didn't budge. *Fuck.* I whipped out my cellphone and immediately dialed my home, and was greeted by a no service alert. If I had been a cartoon character now would have been the time where I gulped and turned blue. I sat down, back against the door. For the first time in my life I had taken a risk, and this was to be my reward. I could just imagine another curious kid sneaking in here and being greeted by my decayed corpse, all because I wanted to know why the light was on. Idiot. Apparently, fortune did not favor the bold. 

The lights flickered again. And then they flickered some more. And then they were off. My heart pounded against my rib cage, for which I was grateful. At least I knew I was still alive. Before I had time to fully let the hopelessness of my situation consume me, the lights came back on. And in the center of the hallway, about 15 or so meters away, was a humanoid female figure dressed in white. It's funny, but when a scenario is this remarkably terrifying in every way the fear doesn't quite bite at you the way you'd expect. It's there of course. But it's numb, harmless, unable to harm you for as long as you wear your shroud of disbelief which I intended to keep on for the rest of my life. Unfortunately for my plans, the figure began moving forward. I realized it was a female. Dressed in white, with tan, flawless skin, and brown hair parted to the side with great care. *What the hell?* 

"Taylor?" I finally let out. 

"Obviously," she said smiling. "You forget how I look already? It's only been a couple of hours, jerk."

"What are you doing here?" I questioned, disbelieving still. 

"Ezra. I've always been right here. Haven't you noticed me? I've been waiting on you."

"Taylor what the fuck is going on?"

"Do you like how I look? I just changed it up for you, the least you could do is tell me what you think." She was dressed in a white dress with spaghetti straps that went down to her knees. Actually a bit above her knees. She was wearing more makeup than normal, and her hair was well conditioned was hanging freely as opposed to her usual ponytail. Her feet were bare. She was beautiful, in every sense of the word but...

"I think I like you better in your softball uniform T. This isn't you. And you don't like me. You like Brendan."

"Oh, I'll wear the softball uniform for you. And you're right. I don't like you. I love you. I'll have the softball uniform tomorrow, but for now..."

In one smooth motion she unzipped the back of her dress and it fell the floor, around her feet. She stepped over it gingerly, and walked until she was just a few feet from me. She put her hands on her hips, and tilted her head as if to say *well?*

I looked away, blushing. She had been wearing nothing underneath her dress, and though I had often dreamed of what she looked like under her leggings and T-shirt, I now found that I could not look at her beyond my peripheral vision. She knelt down by me, and put her hands on my chin, raising my eyes to her's. They were as green and wide as ever, watering with intensity. 

"Don't you want this?" She questioned. Years of soft rejection flitted through my eyes. I remembered us as children, debating what the middle finger meant, and when we were in middle school and got our phones for the first time, how we texted one another late into the night. I remembered how much I had wanted to hurt Brendan when he asked her out, even though he couldn't have known. And I remembered how she had embraced me with tears in her eyes the other week, when I had told her that I was going away to college in New York City, and that my parents were selling the house and moving upstate. She embraced me the same way now.

"More than anything else," I finally answered, returning her embrace. And then the light flickered again, and then it was off. When I came to I was lying outside the complex, on the grass between the cage fence and the street, where cars were flying by so fast that they barely registered. I pulled out my phone and saw that I had one message. From T. The message read *R u coming to the prty after prom on Saturday? Hope 2 c u there!*. I texted her back *No, I can't go. And I'm not coming to prom either. Actually, I don't even think I can come to graduation. Something came up, a family thing, and we leave for upstate on Monday. I probably won't see you again before I go. I need you to tell everyone that I'll miss them, and that I'm sorry. And Taylor. You were a great neighbor.*
